passage:
"Ankita, it's two in the morning. Still on the lab report?"
"Just checking the formatting, Ma."
Jyoti sat on the bed. "You checked it at dinner too."
"There might be a mistake."
"And if there is?"
Ankita's hands stopped on the keyboard. "Then they'll see."
"See what?"
"That I'm normal. Everyone's always said I'm the one who never makes mistakes. Since school. You, Papa, my teachers."
Jyoti was quiet. "We said that because we were proud."
"I know. But now if I get one thing wrong, I'm just ordinary."
"Do you even like chemistry anymore?"
Ankita laughed shakily. "I don't know. I don't have time to think about liking it. I'm too busy not failing."
Jyoti closed the laptop gently. "Ordinary is allowed in this house."

qa.q: What was Ankita still checking at two in the morning?
qa.a: The formatting of the lab report.

qa.q: What is Ankita afraid a single mistake would show?
qa.a: That Ankita is ordinary; the family's pride in never making mistakes has become something to protect, so fear drives the checking more than love of chemistry.

qa.q: What choice by Jyoti helps, and why?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and saying ordinary is allowed, which separates Ankita's worth at home from flawless work.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel on hearing "too busy not failing"?
qa.a: Jyoti seems saddened to realise the family's proud praise became a weight, and wants to lift it.

grounding: A student praised for never making mistakes checks work obsessively, driven by fear of seeming ordinary.

passage: I've been the "perfect one" since Class 4, when my teacher held up my notebook as the model for the whole school. After that, every page, every test, every project had to be flawless. In college it got worse. I'd spend three nights on a two-page assignment, not because I loved the topic but because I was terrified of the one red mark that would prove I was just average. My friend Manoj once asked, "Dhruv, do you actually enjoy economics?" I didn't know how to answer. I think I used to. Somewhere the love got replaced by fear. Last month I handed in an essay with a typo on page one, by accident. Nothing happened. The professor gave it an A. I felt oddly empty, and oddly free.

qa.q: How long would Dhruv spend on a two-page assignment?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel empty and free after the typo essay got an A?
qa.a: The feared disaster didn't happen, which exposed how much of the effort was fear; that was unsettling and a relief at once.

qa.q: What choice could Dhruv make with the next assignment?
qa.a: Set a time limit and submit a solid version on purpose, to test again whether small flaws really prove anything.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Dhruv's hard work?
qa.a: Manoj seems to sense that Dhruv's striving comes from pressure rather than enjoyment, and the question suggests real concern.

grounding: A student praised since childhood for flawless work strives out of fear of being average rather than love of the subject.

passage:
Teacher's note, Hafsa, Kathak senior batch, 4 March
Noor has been with me since she was eight, and for years everyone, including me, praised her as "flawless". Today in rehearsal she missed one turn in the new piece, stopped dead and asked to leave. In the corridor she was shaking. She said, "If I make mistakes on stage, people will see I'm just average. That's all I have." I've noticed she hasn't smiled while dancing for months; she dances as if she's sitting an exam. I think our praise may have taught her that her worth lies in never slipping.
What I did: I asked her to dance the piece once for me with the goal of enjoying it, not getting it right, and told her plainly that I value her whether she slips or not. We'll try again on Thursday.

qa.q: What happened when Noor missed one turn in rehearsal?
qa.a: She stopped dead and asked to leave, and was shaking in the corridor.

qa.q: Why does one missed turn feel so dangerous to Noor?
qa.a: Years of being called flawless made perfection feel like her whole value, so a slip seems to prove she is only average.

qa.q: Which choice by Hafsa addresses the fear behind the perfectionism?
qa.a: Asking her to dance once for enjoyment and saying clearly that she is valued whether she slips or not.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see her own part in Noor's fear?
qa.a: Hafsa admits the years of "flawless" praise, including her own, may have taught Noor that her worth depends on never slipping.

grounding: A dance teacher notes that a student long praised as flawless now dances out of fear of seeming ordinary.

passage:
Sunday, 2 a.m.
Fourth draft of the history seminar paper. Neelam finished hers on Friday and went to the movies. I couldn't. Every paragraph has to be the kind that makes Professor Rao say "excellent" like he did in first year. Since then I've been "the one who never makes mistakes". They say it at home too.
The truth, which I only write here: I'm not sure I even like history anymore. I like not being caught. If one footnote is wrong, everyone will see I'm ordinary, just a normal student who got lucky with praise.
Neelam messaged: "Don't you enjoy it at all?" I didn't answer. I used to. In school I read about the Cholas for fun, under the blanket with a torch.
Maybe I can find that again.
- Gargi

qa.q: What did Neelam do after finishing on Friday?
qa.a: Neelam went to the movies.

qa.q: What does Gargi seem to feel is really driving the fourth draft?
qa.a: Fear more than love: Gargi writes that the real goal is 'not being caught', dreading that one wrong footnote will reveal someone ordinary.

qa.q: What small step could help Gargi reconnect with the subject?
qa.a: Choose one topic to read just for fun, like the Cholas under the blanket, with no marks attached, and set a limit on drafts for the seminar paper.

qa.q: What might Neelam be wondering when asking 'Don't you enjoy it at all?'
qa.a: Neelam seems to sense that the work has become all pressure and no pleasure for Gargi, and may be worried about a friend awake at 2 a.m. on a fourth draft.

grounding: A student long praised for flawless work keeps redrafting out of fear of seeming ordinary rather than love of the subject.

passage: Vandana, you ask why I'm happy when your drawings have mistakes? Let me tell you about my college years in Mysuru. Since primary school, everyone had said, "Chetan never makes a mistake." Neat notebooks, full marks, perfect projects. In engineering college, I kept it up. But I wasn't enjoying anything. I checked every assignment five times. When a friend asked me to join the robotics club, I said no. What if my robot failed in front of everyone? Then they'd see I was ordinary. In third year, I got one question wrong in a test, just one, and I couldn't sleep for two nights. My roommate found me at three in the morning, redoing the problem again and again. He said, "Chetan bhai, do you even like this subject?" I didn't know. I had only ever been afraid of losing it.

qa.q: What did everyone say about Chetan since primary school?
qa.a: "Chetan never makes a mistake."

qa.q: Why did young Chetan refuse to join the robotics club?
qa.a: He was afraid that failing in front of everyone would reveal he was ordinary, so striving was driven by fear, not enjoyment.

passage: The design studio closed at nine, and Sahil still had the model on the table, with the jury the next morning. He had been praised all through school for perfect work, and in architecture college everyone expected his models to be the best. Tonight a wall of his foam model had a slight tilt, maybe two millimetres. His friend Jasleen said it was fine. "No one will see it." "I'll see it," he said. The watchman was locking up. He carried the model back to the hostel in the rain, covering it with his jacket, and rebuilt the wall until four. Jasleen texted, "Do you even enjoy this anymore?" He stared at the message. He didn't answer. The honest answer was no. He only knew he couldn't bear anyone seeing him as ordinary.

qa.q: What was wrong with Sahil's foam model?
qa.a: A wall had a slight tilt, maybe two millimetres.

qa.q: Why did Sahil rebuild the wall until four?
qa.a: He felt afraid that any flaw would show he was ordinary, so fear pushed him harder than enjoyment.

qa.q: What could help Sahil see his work differently?
qa.a: Letting one small flaw go at a jury and noticing that nothing terrible happens could loosen the fear, and talking to a mentor could help.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel reading Sahil's silence?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel worried and a bit helpless, sensing that her friend is driven by fear, not love of design.

grounding: It shows a student praised for flawless work who fears any mistake will reveal he is ordinary, so striving is fuelled by fear.

passage: Damini had been the topper since Class 1, and now, in her second year of economics at a Mumbai college, she was still getting perfect grades. Her friend Farhan asked her to co-write a paper for a student conference, something new and risky. Damini said no. "I'm busy." Really, she was scared. What if the idea failed? What if people saw that she was just good at exams and not truly brilliant? She stayed with safe assignments. At night she reread her old praise-filled report cards and felt a strange mixture of pride and dread. When Farhan's paper won a prize, she clapped, but her stomach twisted. She hadn't even tried. She realised she couldn't remember the last time she had enjoyed economics. She had only been afraid of not being the best at it.

qa.q: What did Farhan ask Damini to do?
qa.a: Co-write a paper for a student conference.

qa.q: Why did Damini say she was busy?
qa.a: She felt scared that a risky idea might fail and show she was ordinary, so fear of losing her image kept her away.

qa.q: What could Damini try to reconnect with enjoying economics?
qa.a: She could take one small risk, like helping with a section of a new paper, and focus on the ideas instead of the grade.

qa.q: How might Farhan see Damini's refusal?
qa.a: Farhan might think Damini is simply busy or uninterested, not knowing about her fear.

grounding: It shows a student always praised for perfect grades who fears any mistake will reveal she is ordinary, so her striving is driven by fear.

passage:
In school I was the one with the perfect notebooks. Teachers held them up. My parents framed my certificates. I'm Manjula, and I learned early that flawless was who I was.
In college, that became a cage. I'd spend six hours on an assignment that needed two. I'd redo a lab report because one graph wasn't centred. My friend Swati once said, “You don't seem to enjoy any of this.”
She was right. I didn't. I was too busy being afraid.
Afraid that one mistake would reveal the truth: that I was ordinary, and all the praise had been a misunderstanding.
I remember handing in a history essay with a small spelling error I'd missed. I didn't sleep that night. The professor didn't even mark it.
Looking back, I think I loved learning once. The fear pushed it out.

qa.q: How long would Manjula spend on an assignment that needed two hours?
qa.a: Manjula would spend six hours on it.

qa.q: Why did Manjula lose sleep over one spelling error?
qa.a: Manjula was afraid that any mistake would reveal Manjula as ordinary and prove the praise had been a misunderstanding.

qa.q: What could help Manjula rediscover a love of learning?
qa.a: Setting time limits, allowing small imperfections, and perhaps talking to a counsellor about the fear behind the striving.

qa.q: How does Swati see Manjula's work habits?
qa.a: Swati notices that Manjula doesn't seem to enjoy any of it, and seems concerned.

grounding: The reflection shows a student long praised for flawless work fearing that any mistake will reveal ordinariness, with fear pushing out love of learning.

passage:
Faculty mentor's note, second-year B.Arch, October.
Hrithik has the most detailed drawings in his batch and is regularly praised by the jury. He also submits almost everything late, because he redraws plates until they are “perfect.”
Today he came to me visibly anxious. A small dimension error had been found in his last plate. He said, “Everyone thinks I'm the best. If they see mistakes, they'll realise I'm not.”
His friend Zainab, who was with him, said he hasn't enjoyed a single project this semester, only worried about them.
It seems the striving is powered by fear rather than love of the work.
What I did next: I told him that one dimension error does not undo two years of good work, and that I value his ideas more than flawless lines. I have suggested he see the college counsellor about the anxiety, and set him a limit of two drafts per plate for the next month.

qa.q: What error had been found in Hrithik's plate?
qa.a: A small dimension error in his last plate.

qa.q: Why was Hrithik so anxious about the small error?
qa.a: He feared that any mistake would reveal he isn't the best, so his striving is driven by fear.

qa.q: What did the mentor suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Seeing the college counsellor and a two-draft limit per plate, to ease the fear and loosen the need for perfection.

qa.q: How does Zainab see Hrithik's semester?
qa.a: Zainab sees that he has only worried, not enjoyed, his projects, and seems concerned.

grounding: The mentor's note shows a student praised for flawless work fearing mistakes will reveal him as ordinary, his striving fuelled by fear.

passage:
Monday night
I haven't told anyone this, not even Yogesh. I'm Imran, and I've been the "flawless" one since Class 5. Full marks, neat notebooks, teachers reading my answers aloud.
Today the professor returned the first econometrics assignment with one red mark: a small slip in a formula. Everyone else had ten. I had one. And my stomach dropped as if I'd failed the year.
I rewrote the whole thing tonight even though it isn't being regraded.
Here's the truth: I don't do this because I love economics. I used to. Now it's fear. If I make a mistake, then maybe I'm just ordinary, and everything people praised me for was fake.
Yogesh makes mistakes all the time and laughs. He seems to enjoy the subject more than I do. That's the part that scares me most.

qa.q: How many red marks did Imran get on the assignment?
qa.a: Imran got one red mark, for a small slip in a formula.

qa.q: Why did one red mark make Imran's stomach drop?
qa.a: Imran feels afraid that any mistake would reveal being ordinary, so even one error feels like failing the year.

qa.q: What small step could Imran take to loosen this fear?
qa.a: Imran could talk honestly to Yogesh or a counsellor about the fear, and try leaving one small mistake uncorrected to see that nothing terrible happens.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see mistakes differently from Imran?
qa.a: Yogesh makes mistakes and laughs, treating them as part of learning, which is why he seems to enjoy the subject more.

grounding: It shows a student praised for flawless work fearing that any mistake will reveal they are ordinary, so the striving is driven by fear more than love of the subject.

passage:
In the small college in Bhilwara, Raghav was the name every lecturer knew. First in every exam since school, handwriting like print, answers read out in class.
On the day of the physics practical, his circuit didn't work. He checked it five times. His hands started shaking. Around him, other students' bulbs glowed.
His friend Harsha leaned over. "Loose wire, probably. Happens to everyone."
Raghav didn't hear. He was thinking: if I fail this, everyone will know I was never really good. Just lucky, or just careful.
The lecturer came over, found the loose wire in ten seconds, and moved on without a word.
On the walk home, Harsha said, "You used to love fixing circuits. You made that doorbell for your Dadi."
"That was for fun," Raghav said. "Now it's not allowed to go wrong."

qa.q: What was wrong with Raghav's circuit?
qa.a: The lecturer found a loose wire.

qa.q: What was Raghav afraid of when the circuit didn't work?
qa.a: He was frightened that one failure would show everyone he was never really good, just lucky or careful.

qa.q: What could help Raghav enjoy physics again?
qa.a: He could practise building circuits just for fun again, like the doorbell, and talk to Harsha or a teacher about how the fear of mistakes has taken over.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the loose wire?
qa.a: Harsha sees it as an ordinary slip that happens to everyone, and is concerned that Raghav reacts so strongly.

grounding: It shows a student praised for flawless work fearing any mistake will expose him as ordinary, so the striving is fed by fear instead of love of the work.

passage:
Copenhagen was dark by half past three that December, and the student kitchen smelled of Omar's mulled juice. Emil sat at the table with his thesis draft and a red pen.
"You got a twelve on every exam since first year," Omar said. "Why are you rewriting the introduction again?"
"Because they expect it now." Emil's pen hovered. "If this is just okay, everyone will see I was never special. I was just careful."
"Do you even like the topic?"
Emil paused. He used to. In second year he'd stayed up reading about harbour cities for fun. Now he mostly felt his stomach tighten when he opened the file.
"I'll like it when it's perfect," he said, and crossed out a sentence that had been fine.
Omar pushed a mug toward him and said nothing.

qa.q: What grade had Emil got on every exam since first year?
qa.a: He had got a twelve on every exam since first year.

qa.q: What is Emil afraid of as he keeps rewriting the introduction?
qa.a: He is afraid that any ordinary draft will show he was never special, so fear, more than love of the topic, is pushing him.

qa.q: What could Emil try to reconnect with why he chose this work?
qa.a: He could spend a little time reading about harbour cities just for interest again, and set a clear point where the introduction counts as done.

qa.q: How might Omar feel as he pushes the mug toward Emil and stays quiet?
qa.a: Omar is probably worried and caring, unsure how to help a friend who can't enjoy work he used to love.

grounding: A student praised for flawless work fears any mistake will expose him as ordinary, so fear now fuels his striving.
